//: Railway deployment for the web app. Committed rather than configured only in the
dashboard, because a build command that exists solely in somebody's browser is a
build command nobody can review and nobody can restore.
The mobile app is not deployed from here — it ships through EAS to the stores and
talks to the same Supabase project directly.
Full procedure, including the Supabase side, in docs/deploy-railway.md.
JUST `npm run build`. An earlier version was `npm ci --include=dev && npm run build`,
which FAILED THE FIRST DEPLOY, and the reasoning behind it was wrong twice over.
The claim was that Nixpacks sets NODE_ENV=production, so npm would omit
devDependencies and `next build` would fail on a missing typescript. Neither half held.
Nixpacks runs its own install phase — plain `npm ci` — and the build log shows it adding
898 packages against 903 in the lockfile, so dev dependencies were already there. And
typescript, @types/react and @types/node are not dev-only in this lockfile anyway; they
are reachable through non-dev edges, so `--omit=dev` would not have dropped them.
What the redundant command actually did was fail. `npm ci` deletes node_modules before
reinstalling, and the second run hit a directory the builder was still holding:
npm error code EBUSY
npm error EBUSY: resource busy or locked, rmdir '/app/node_modules/.cache'
Belt-and-braces against a failure mode that did not exist, which caused one that did.
If a future builder ever does prune dev dependencies, the fix is the Railway variable
NPM_CONFIG_INCLUDE=dev — not a second install.
`npm run build` at the root builds core, then api, then web, in that order: the two
packages ship TypeScript source and are transpiled by Next, so their `build` scripts
are typechecks. Web last, because it depends on both.
The NEXT_PUBLIC_* variables must exist at BUILD time, not just at runtime — Next
inlines them into the client bundle. A deploy that has them only as runtime
variables produces a browser bundle pointing at `undefined`.
`next start` needs no port flag: it reads PORT (commander `.env('PORT')`, default
3000) and binds 0.0.0.0 by default. Verified rather than assumed — PORT=3999 and it
served on 3999.
The workspace flag matters: `npm run start` at the root has no start script, and
`cd apps/web && npm start` loses npm's workspace symlinks for @ece/core and @ece/api.

The coupling runs both ways and there is no way to express it in this file: Railway's
config cannot read an environment variable. So if ECE_PORTAL_MOUNT is ever cleared —
when Doorway gets a domain of its own and the console moves back to its own root — this
path must lose the prefix in the SAME change, or the deploy that removes the mount will
fail its health check. Loud, but only if somebody reads this.
//restart: ON_FAILURE with a small retry count. Not ALWAYS: this process has no reason to exit
on its own, so an exit is a fault, and restarting it forever turns a crash loop into
a quiet one that looks like uptime.
